evidence_notes.finding: This doctoral research plan argues that a driver/navigator multi-agent pair only earns trust over a single-agent setup when the navigator's critique is constrained to machine-checkable contracts and formal specifications validated by deterministic verifiers, rather than free-form LLM judgment. Preliminary verifier-guided specification synthesis (AutoReSpec, AutoJML) is offered as evidence that iterative verifier feedback improves correctness and completeness.
evidence_notes.quote: We will study a driver-and-navigator setup to quantify when multi-agent collaboration improves reliability and trust signals relative to single-agent baselines.

extraction.framework: Driver-navigator LLM pair-programming MAS; preliminary systems AutoReSpec and AutoJML for JML specification synthesis
extraction.baseline: single-agent / single-stage specification and repair setups; prior state-of-the-art specification generators
extraction.key_results: AutoReSpec verified 67 of 72 programs with 58.2% success probability and 69.2% completeness while cutting average evaluation time by 26.89% over prior methods; AutoJML verified 109 of 120 programs with 79.3% average completeness, including 81.48% on multi-path loops and 85.71% on nested loops. The proposed contribution is shifting trust from one model's assessment of another to externally verifiable solver-backed evidence (proofs or counterexamples).
extraction.limitations: The three planned studies (requirements/specification translation, TDD refinement, maintenance) are not yet executed, so the multi-agent trust claim is unvalidated. The author explicitly flags the risk that an LLM navigator merely trades one auditability problem for another, and evidence so far is confined to specification synthesis on small program benchmarks rather than repository-scale evolution.

evidence_notes.finding: A single tool-calling LLM agent closes a detect-diagnose-remediate loop over a K3s cloud-edge cluster, but reliability is strongly model-dependent: GPT-5 identifies faults far more accurately and in roughly half the reasoning rounds of the GPT-5-mini baseline, and the binary success metric can score a run successful even when root-cause identification was 0%.
evidence_notes.quote: Results show that the agent identifies SLA violations with 52.9% accuracy and mitigates 70.7% of them successfully.

extraction.framework: ARM (Autonomous Remediation & Management), a closed-loop intent-driven agent using Prometheus monitoring and a Model Context Protocol server exposing kubectl, observability and autoscaling tools
extraction.agent_count: 1 (single LLM control agent with tool calling)
extraction.benchmark: Custom reproducible chaos fault-injection suite on a K3s Kubernetes cluster: pod/node CPU stress, memory stress and pod disruption across three synthetic IoT applications (IoT Gateway 3 services, Smart Manufacturing 7, Smart City 12), 20 experiments per application
extraction.baseline: GPT-5-mini as a lighter-weight agent baseline running the same topologies, fault injections and tools
extraction.key_results: GPT-5 restores SLA metrics in roughly 80% of fault-injection runs and correctly identifies the underlying condition in about 78% of cases. GPT-5 reaches 100% identification on the no-failure baseline and node CPU stress where GPT-5-mini reaches 0.0% and 88.9%; GPT-5 completes pod-level incidents in 10.2-23.0 reasoning rounds versus 27.7-34.2 for the mini model. Latency Recovery shows 80.4% (GPT-5) versus 79.4% (mini) of CPU-stress degradation reclaimed despite moderate binary success. Observability tool calls dominate interaction volume relative to actuation.
extraction.limitations: Non-negligible wall-clock remediation times for the largest topology and a distinct performance gap between model sizes, implying frontier-class models are currently required for zero-touch control. Remediation success is scored purely from latency and success-rate recovery, so subtle faults can yield 100% success with 0% identification accuracy, overstating capability. Evaluation uses emulated stressors on a constrained single cluster where resource exhaustion makes exact baseline recovery physically infeasible; safety safeguards around high-impact actions are left to future work.

evidence_notes.finding: A taxonomic review contrasting human-in-the-loop 'vibe coding' with autonomous 'agentic coding', arguing that agentic scalability will come from orchestrator-coordinated specialized sub-agents rather than a monolithic agent, while cataloguing agentic failure modes of overdependence, silent error propagation across modules, and expanded runtime privilege as security surface.
evidence_notes.quote: Scalability in agentic coding will emerge not from a single monolithic agent, but from a constellation of specialized sub-agents planners, coders, testers, reviewers coordinated by an orchestrator.

extraction.baseline: vibe coding (prompt-based, conversational, human-in-the-loop) compared against agentic coding (goal-driven, autonomous, tool-executing)
extraction.key_results: Proposes a taxonomy across conceptual foundations, execution models, feedback loops, safety mechanisms, debugging strategies and tool ecosystems, illustrated with 20 use cases. Vibe systems are positioned for prototyping, ideation and education; agentic systems for enterprise automation, codebase refactoring and CI/CD integration through in-sandbox execution, embedded validation, namespace isolation, resource limits, logging hooks and rollback triggers. The roadmap calls for shared communication protocols, task-graph serialization, contextual memory sharing, persistent memory and human-AI supervision infrastructure, concluding that success depends on harmonizing both paradigms rather than choosing one.
extraction.limitations: A conceptual review with no new empirical evaluation, benchmark measurement or controlled comparison; claims about relative paradigm strength rest on secondary literature and illustrative use cases. Identified risks are stated qualitatively: agentic overdependence and skill atrophy, silent cross-module error propagation without rollback or observability hooks, prompt injection and secret leakage from expanded runtime privileges, and for vibe coding, black-box generation, output stochasticity under near-identical prompts, poor integration with production systems, and code-quality drift.

evidence_notes.finding: A single LLM instructed against the ISO 29148 quality characteristics achieves high recall but low precision when human software engineers are treated as ground truth, so it works as a reviewer aid that surfaces candidate flaws with plausible explanations rather than as an autonomous quality gate.
evidence_notes.quote: The current capabilities of LLMs are not sufficient to fully automate this task.

extraction.framework: Llama 2 prompted to assess, explain and improve individual requirement statements against the nine ISO 29148 quality characteristics
extraction.benchmark: Requirement sets from a hypothetical Stopwatch project and the real-world DigitalHome project, evaluated over the nine ISO 29148 characteristics
extraction.baseline: assessments by human study participants with a software engineering background, used as ground truth; independent versus bound (LLM-informed) assessment phases
extraction.key_results: Recall is high (0.7414-1.0) while precision is low in the independent phase (0.1257 DigitalHome, 0.50 Stopwatch) and rises in the bound phase (0.3214 and 0.8837). Cohen's Kappa shows weak or non-existent participant-LLM agreement independently but increases once participants see the LLM decision and explanation. Explanations were judged plausible for 70-100% of characteristics, and LLM-proposed rewrites were judged improvements in most characteristics (50-100%). In Stopwatch, LLM false flags fell from 25 of 90 items to 5 between the independent and bound phases.
extraction.limitations: Only one hypothetical and one real project, both relatively simple, limiting generalizability; token limits for larger project descriptions were not addressed. A single model (Llama 2) and a single prompt template were tested, so results cannot be generalized across LLMs or prompting strategies. Precision is computed against participant judgments that themselves shift after exposure to the LLM output, and the LLM was instructed to fix one characteristic at a time rather than produce an overall improved requirement.

evidence_notes.finding: In a controlled ablation on the same task subset, the role-specialized multi-agent configuration beat direct single-agent tool integration only for the strongest model (GPT-4o, 70% vs 58% success); weaker models showed minimal difference because they failed the cross-domain coordination the topology was meant to exploit, and single-agent architectures retained the compute and latency advantage.
evidence_notes.quote: These findings indicate that while computational efficiency favours single-agent implementations, the enhanced coordination capabilities of multi-agent frameworks provide measurable performance gains for advanced models capable of complex reasoning.

extraction.framework: AILA (Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant): a LangGraph planner that dynamically routes between an AFM Handler Agent and a Data Handler Agent via NEED HELP / FINAL ANSWER keywords, with an MCP reimplementation used as a framework cross-check
extraction.agent_count: 3 (planner plus AFM Handler Agent and Data Handler Agent)
extraction.benchmark: AFMBench, 100 expert-curated atomic force microscopy tasks executed on real hardware; 17% require multi-agent coordination; single-vs-multi ablation on a 10-question subset with 3 independent trials each
extraction.baseline: single-agent multi-tool AILA with direct tool integration; also cross-model comparison of GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Claude-3.5-sonnet and Llama-3.3-70B
extraction.key_results: GPT-4o achieved 70% success in the multi-agent configuration versus 58% with direct tool integration, while other models showed minimal framework-dependent difference. GPT-4o reached 65% overall task success at 5.96 steps per task versus 10.21 steps for Llama-3.3-70B; total error rates were 29% (GPT-4o), 51.7% (Claude-3.5), 60.7% (Llama-3.3-70B) and 66.7% (GPT-3.5). Claude-3.5's failures were dominated by agent-selection errors (28.3%), consistently misdelegating between the AFM and Data handlers, whereas GPT-4o's were dominated by code generation (21.7%) and instruction adherence (15%). Debugging failures resolve into iteration-limit exhaustion and instruction overreach; agents also exhibited 'sleepwalking', taking unauthorized actions such as risky tip movements.
extraction.limitations: The single-versus-multi comparison rests on only 10 questions with 3 trials each. Significant prompt fragility means small prompt-structure changes cause substantial performance swings even in GPT-4o. Domain question-answering proficiency does not predict agentic capability (Claude-3.5 underperformed despite strong materials QA scores), and the instruction-adherence deviations raise unresolved safety-alignment risks for hardware-in-the-loop laboratory settings.

evidence_notes.finding: Test insufficiency in the standard HumanEval suite inflates measured correctness and, more damagingly for comparative claims, reorders model rankings: augmenting tests 80x drops pass@k by up to 19.3-28.9% and flips which models appear best.
evidence_notes.quote: We also surprisingly found that test insufficiency can lead to mis-ranking.

extraction.framework: EvalPlus, combining ChatGPT-seeded input generation with type-aware mutation to augment code benchmarks; produces HumanEval+ and HumanEval+-Mini
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval and the augmented HumanEval+ (80x more test cases, 83 of 164 tasks annotated with hand-crafted contracts), evaluated over 26 LLMs
extraction.baseline: the original HumanEval test suite and its reported pass@k
extraction.key_results: pass@k falls consistently under HumanEval+, by up to 23.1% (pass@1 greedy), 19.3% (pass@1), 24.9% (pass@10) and 28.9% (pass@100), including 12.6% for ChatGPT and 13.1% for GPT-4, 18.5% for CodeGen-16B, 17.6% for CodeLlama-34B and 14.1% for StarCoder. Over 10% of the original HumanEval ground-truth solutions were found to be incorrectly implemented and were reimplemented. Test insufficiency causes mis-ranking: WizardCoder-CodeLlama and Phind-CodeLlama outrank ChatGPT on HumanEval+ but not on HumanEval. HumanEval+-Mini is 47x smaller while preserving similar test effectiveness.
extraction.limitations: The approach gives no formal correctness guarantee; it cross-checks against manually re-implemented ground truths and hand-written contracts covering only about half the tasks, and input generation runs under a one-hour budget per task. Only HumanEval is extended in this work; MBPP and formal or translation-validation integration are left as future work.

Verbal self-reflection over an episodic memory buffer lifts a single agent to 91.0 pass@1 on HumanEval versus 80.1 for GPT-4, but the gain is bounded by the quality of the agent's self-generated tests: on MBPP Python a 16.3% false-positive test rate makes Reflexion underperform its own baseline, and ablating test generation drops accuracy below baseline (52% vs 60%).
evidence_notes.quote: We acknowledge that self-reflecting code-generation agents are bound to their ability to write diverse, comprehensive tests.

extraction.framework: Reflexion: an Actor, an Evaluator and a Self-Reflection model coupled to an episodic memory buffer, using verbal rather than gradient reinforcement
extraction.agent_count: 1 agent composed of 3 model roles (Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection), memory limited to 1 experience for programming
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval (Python and Rust), MBPP (Python and Rust), LeetcodeHardGym (40 post-cutoff Leetcode hard problems), HotPotQA, AlfWorld
extraction.baseline: single-sample zero-shot code generation with GPT-4; prior SOTA including CodeT+GPT-3.5 and ReAct-style decision-making agents
extraction.key_results: HumanEval Python 91.0 pass@1 versus 80.1 GPT-4 SOTA; HumanEval Rust 68.0 versus 60.0; MBPP Rust 75.4 versus 70.9; Leetcode Hard 15.0 versus 7.5; MBPP Python 77.1 versus 80.1, the one regression. AlfWorld improves by an absolute 22% over strong baselines in 12 learning steps and HotPotQA by 20%. Ablation on the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems: full Reflexion 0.68, omitting test generation 0.52 (below the 0.60 baseline), omitting self-reflection 0.60 (no gain), indicating blind trial-and-error debugging without reflection is ineffective on harder tasks.
extraction.limitations: As natural-language policy optimization it can settle in non-optimal local minima and offers no formal success guarantee, depending on the LLM's own self-evaluation. Long-term memory is a fixed-capacity sliding window. Self-generated test suites produce false positives (16.3% on MBPP Python versus 1.4% on HumanEval Python), causing premature invalid submissions; test-driven specification also breaks down for non-deterministic generators, impure API-calling functions, hardware-dependent output and concurrent behavior.

Human-oriented programming grammar imposes a measurable token tax on LLM inference; an AI-oriented grammar (SimPy) that preserves the Python AST cuts token usage by 13.5% (CodeLlama) and 10.4% (GPT-4) while models trained Python-then-SimPy match or exceed their Python baselines.
evidence_notes.quote: In the experiments, compared with Python, SimPy enables a reduction in token usage by 13.5% and 10.4% for CodeLlama and GPT-4, respectively, when completing the same set of code-related tasks.

extraction.framework: SimPy, an AI-oriented Python grammar with an identical AST and a bidirectional converter, plus the DualCode inference framework that shows humans Python while models consume SimPy
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval (Pass@1, Pass@10) plus a real-world repository code corpus for token-reduction measurement across CodeLlama, WizardCoder, GPT-4 and other tokenizers
extraction.baseline: standard human-centric Python grammar and models trained on Python
extraction.key_results: Token reduction of 12.6-13.5% across tokenizers, including 13.5% for CodeLlama and WizardCoder and 10.4% for GPT-4. Training directly on SimPy alone hurts accuracy (CodeGen 2.93% Pass@1 and 5.49% Pass@10 versus 4.51% and 7.32% for Python), but sequential Python-then-SimPy training matches or beats the Python control: CodeGen-NL 9.15%, TinyLlama 14.02% and Pythia 10.00% Pass@10 versus 7.32%, 13.41% and 9.76%. DualCode conversion latency stays under 1 ms for code up to 500 tokens, and over 95% of real-world files fall within the 5000-token range.
extraction.limitations: Fine-tuning experiments are restricted to roughly 1B-parameter models by available compute, so conclusions may not transfer to larger models. Only Python is implemented, so generalization to other languages is untested. The proof-of-concept converter is written in Python and is unoptimized, likely underestimating achievable performance. DualCode's AST-based converter requires grammatically correct input, limiting use for partial-code tasks such as code completion, and effective SimPy fine-tuning required the full dataset.

evidence_notes.finding: Wrapping a single LLM in a debugger-grounded hypothesis-experiment-observation loop yields repair performance competitive with direct LLM patch generation while producing explanations that improved developer patch-correctness judgments in five of six real-world bugs, at a cost of 4.66x longer runtime and a regression on Defects4J v1.2.
evidence_notes.quote: in our experiments, AutoSDtook on average 4.66 times longer to generate a patch when compared to LLM- Base.

extraction.framework: AutoSD (Automated Scientific Debugging): an LLM prompted to generate hypotheses and debugger scripts, execute them via pdb/jdb, and reach explicit conclusions before patch generation
extraction.benchmark: Defects4J v1.2 and v2.0, the newly constructed ARHE benchmark, and BugsInPy for the human study; plus a 20-participant user study including six professional developers
extraction.baseline: LLM-Base direct patch generation, a template-based baseline, Recoder, fine-tuned InCoder, Codex and ChatRepair
extraction.key_results: AutoSD fixes 113 bugs on Defects4J v2.0 versus 110 for LLM-Base, 48 for ChatRepair and 45 for Codex, but 76 versus 87 for LLM-Base on v1.2, with the shortfall concentrated in the Closure project's nested reference structures; it matches or beats Codex and ChatRepair using 10 rather than 200 patch candidates. The self-emitted <DONE> token is a usable confidence signal: 89% of plausible patches with <DONE> were correct versus 82% without. Ablating real debugger execution ('debugger hallucination') drops the plausible-patch rate from 73% to 63% and inverts the <DONE> signal from +12.4pp to -11pp. In the human study, participants with explanations judged patch correctness more accurately in five of six bugs, 70% wanted explanations from repair tools and 55% were satisfied with the Scientific Debugging presentation.
extraction.limitations: Multi-step model and debugger invocation makes AutoSD 4.66x slower than LLM-Base (9m22s versus 1m59s for ten patches). It assumes method-level fault localization and handles only single-method bugs, and is evaluated only on Python and Java. Generated explanations may occasionally lend credibility to incorrect patches. Threats include possible training-data leakage from Defects4J (partly mitigated by the new ARHE benchmark), inaccurate patch-correctness assessment, and potential bias in the human study.
